2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern: eligibility required availability for the full study duration, and all 8 enrolled co-researchers completed training, 5-day photo collection (281 total photographs across the two groups), gallery-walk selection, and group dialogue sessions, although pre-enrollment refusal counts during health-center candidate identification are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable in causal/statistical terms (primary qualitative phenomenological study with no quantitative effect estimation); contextual seasonal, environmental, household, and gendered socio-cultural factors shaping postpartum water access and workload are explored narratively.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / incidental (not a legal-empirical study): formal law and policy (such as the Government of Malawi's 2022 Revised National Water Policy and women's exclusion from formal water governance structures) appear only as background framing, while primary empirical observations capture informal village household water-separation rules, gendered domestic and school/facility labor norms, and collective community well-digging practices via participant narratives.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: participant-led photography, Chichewa-language PHOTO group discussions, co-researcher captioning, and community exhibition validation strengthen credibility, but the unplanned attendance of three local leaders during workshops introduces potential authority/social-desirability bias, and the paper does not report whether Chichewa discussions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, or back-translated.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for qualitative lived-experience inquiry, weak for clinical or microbiological outcomes: household water acquisition barriers, queueing, seasonal river hazards, rationing trade-offs, psychosocial stress, and infant/maternal hygiene compromises are richly documented through 44 selected photographs and narratives across all 8 co-researchers, whereas water contamination and maternal/newborn health conditions (e.g., cholera, infections, rashes) rely on self-reported perceptions rather than objective clinical or water-quality testing.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: no pre-registered qualitative protocol is cited, but the authors transparently report how 281 photographs were narrowed by co-researchers to 44 images (Table 1), include voices from all 8 coded co-researchers alongside community validation, and explicitly explain privacy-based exclusion of identifiable faces or sensitive images.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern (inherent to small purposive participatory design): 8 women (4 postpartum mothers and 4 female guardians, aged 20-43) were purposively selected from two high-vulnerability health facility catchment areas (Chimvu and Thekerani) in Thyolo District in consultation with local health centers based on recent facility delivery, availability, and willingness to share with outsiders, which suits exploratory photovoice inquiry but excludes mothers delivering outside facilities or unable to attend workshops and limits broader transferability.

domain_ratings.justification: The abstract and introduction clearly state the research goal: to understand how postpartum women in rural Malawi meet their water needs, examine factors shaping water acquisition and utilization, and illuminate lived maternal health experiences to inform the SURG-Water initiative and wider water-insecurity interventions.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This primary qualitative participatory study used photovoice, Chichewa-language gallery walks and PHOTO group discussions, phenomenological coding in NVivo 12, and community validation exhibitions to examine postpartum women's lived experiences of water scarcity in two rural catchment areas of Thyolo District, Malawi (n = 8 female co-researchers: 4 mothers and 4 guardians). Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study raises low-to-moderate methodological concern overall (9 'Yes' and 0 'Can't tell' or 'No' ratings across Q1-Q9, plus clear practical value under Q10). Strengths include transparent alignment between research aims and participatory visual methodology, explicit researcher positionality and anti-colonial partnership framing, clear ethical safeguards for visual data, participant-led selection and captioning of 44 photographs from 281 taken, voices represented across all eight co-researchers, and post-analysis community exhibitions for validation. Key methodological limitations are the small purposive sample recruited via health facilities in high-vulnerability sites, lack of explicit detail on audio-recording and verbatim transcription/translation verification of Chichewa group discussions, potential social desirability or authority bias from the unplanned workshop attendance of three local leaders, and reliance on self-reported perceptions rather than clinical or microbiological measures for health and water-quality outcomes (with formal water law/governance addressed only as background context rather than empirically measured).
raw_response.overall_rating: Low-to-moderate methodological concern (9 Yes, 0 Can't tell / No items across Q1-Q9; minor concerns regarding small health-center-recruited sample, unreported transcription/translation mechanics, and local leaders' unplanned workshop presence)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative participatory study (community-based participatory action research using photovoice, structured group discussions, and phenomenological analysis)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, setting, purposive recruitment criteria, researcher reflexivity, photovoice workshops, phenomenological NVivo 12 analysis, community validation, and ethics are reported in Abstract (PDF Page 1), Section 2 Methods (PDF Pages 2-4), and Ethics statement (PDF Page 13); thematic findings, photo counts (Table 1), and captioned verbatim narratives appear in Section 3 Results (PDF Pages 4-12); methodological limitations and transferability are discussed in Section 4 Discussion (PDF Pages 12-13).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study collects and analyzes exclusively qualitative primary empirical data—participant-generated photographs, Chichewa gallery-walk discussions structured by the PHOTO guide, and phenomenological thematic interpretation—with no quantitative comparator or statistical component (Table 1 merely catalogs photo counts and titles across themes). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the required appraisal tool for primary qualitative designs.
